activities.name: Conversation Rescue
activities.description: Choose a helpful response when a conversation is difficult.

items.context: The line is noisy. You did not hear the last sentence.
items.prompt: Ask the speaker to say the last sentence again.
options: Could you speak about something else?
Could you tell me your opinion?
Could you repeat the last sentence, please?
Could you explain why you called?
items.explanation: “Repeat” asks for the same words again. You need to hear the sentence before discussing its meaning.

items.context: You heard every word, but the speaker is speaking too fast for you to follow.
items.prompt: Ask for a slower speed.
options: Could you speak a little more slowly?
Could you speak a little more loudly?
Could you repeat only the date?
Could you explain what that word means?
items.explanation: “More slowly” changes the speed. “More loudly” changes the volume.

items.context: A person gives an unfamiliar street name. You need to write its letters correctly.
items.prompt: Ask for the spelling.
options: How do you spell that street name?
What does that street name mean?
Could you say the street name more loudly?
Which street comes after that one?
items.explanation: Spelling gives the letters in a word. Distance and length do not help you write its name.

items.context: You heard “fifteen” or “fifty.” You are not sure which number the speaker said.
items.prompt: Check the two possible numbers.
options: Did you mean that fifteen would be enough?
Could we change the number to fifty?
Would you prefer fifteen or fifty?
Did you say fifteen or fifty?
items.explanation: Offering the two possibilities makes the uncertainty clear and easy to answer.

items.context: Someone is speaking very quietly. You can see that they are still talking.
items.prompt: Ask for a louder voice.
options: Could you speak a little more slowly, please?
Could you repeat the first point in simpler words?
Could you explain that last word, please?
Could you speak a little louder, please?
items.explanation: “Louder” asks for more volume. “Later” asks for a different time.

items.context: You heard the meeting time clearly: three o’clock. You did not hear the room number.
items.prompt: Ask only for the detail you missed.
options: Sorry, why is the meeting so long?
Sorry, who chose three o’clock?
Sorry, which room is the meeting in?
Sorry, what time is the meeting?
items.explanation: You already know the time. Ask for the missing room number.

items.context: A video call freezes while someone explains the second step of a task.
items.prompt: Explain the problem and request that step again.
options: The video froze. Could you repeat step two?
I disagree with step two. Please change it.
I finished step two. What comes after it?
The video is clear. Please keep going.
items.explanation: Name the connection problem, then say exactly what you missed. Freezing does not mean you disagree.

items.context: You want to write down an address before the speaker continues.
items.prompt: Ask for a short pause.
options: Could you give me a moment to write that down?
Could you check whether this is your address?
Could you explain how to get to that address?
Could you wait until tomorrow to send the address?
items.explanation: “Give me a moment” asks for a little time. The reason tells the speaker why you need the pause.

items.context: The speaker says “Tuesday,” but you want to confirm that you heard correctly.
items.prompt: Check what you heard without changing it.
options: Did you say Tuesday?
Could we change it to Tuesday?
Would Tuesday be more convenient?
Did we meet there last Tuesday?
items.explanation: “Did you say…?” checks the speaker’s words. A new date would suggest a change instead.

items.context: You heard the price, but you need a written copy to avoid a mistake.
items.prompt: Ask the speaker to send the price in writing.
options: Could you explain how you chose the price?
Could you lower the price for me?
Could you tell me a different price?
Could you send me the price in a message?
items.explanation: The problem is remembering the exact price. Asking for a message does not ask for a discount.

items.context: Someone says “The fee is optional.” You do not know the word “optional.”
items.prompt: Ask about that word’s meaning.
options: Could you say “optional” more loudly?
What does “optional” mean here?
Could you spell “optional” for me?
Could you repeat the amount of the fee?
items.explanation: Name the word you do not understand. The other questions ask about the fee, not the word.

items.context: You understand a general instruction but cannot picture what to do.
items.prompt: Ask for an example.
options: Could you repeat the instruction word for word?
Could you tell me when the task is due?
Could you explain who gave the instruction?
Could you give me an example?
items.explanation: An example shows how an instruction works in a specific case.

items.context: You think the shop closes at six, but you want to check your understanding.
items.prompt: Restate your understanding as a question.
options: The shop should close at seven.
Why does the shop open so early?
I prefer shops that close late.
So the shop closes at six, right?
items.explanation: “So…right?” checks an interpretation. It does not ask the shop to change its hours.

items.context: Someone says “Put it over there.” There are two boxes and several shelves.
items.prompt: Ask which object and place they mean.
options: Which box do you mean, and which shelf?
Which shelf is nearest to the door?
Which box did we use yesterday?
Which shelves have already been filled?
items.explanation: “It” and “there” are unclear. Ask for the object and location directly.

items.context: A colleague says “That works.” You are unsure whether they mean the machine or your plan.
items.prompt: Check what “that” refers to.
options: Are you saying the plan needs to change?
Are you asking when we should start work?
Do you mean the machine works, or the plan is suitable?
Are you asking me to repair the machine?
items.explanation: Give the two possible meanings. Here, “works” can describe functioning or being suitable.

items.context: Someone uses several technical words while explaining a phone problem.
items.prompt: Ask for simpler language.
options: Could you explain that in simpler words?
Could you spell each technical term for me?
Could you repeat the same explanation more loudly?
Could you give me more technical detail?
items.explanation: Simpler words address the language difficulty while keeping the same topic.

items.context: You heard “before Friday.” You need to know whether Friday itself is allowed.
items.prompt: Ask about the time limit precisely.
options: Does that mean I can finish at any time on Friday?
Does that mean I should begin on Friday?
Does that mean you will send it to me on Friday?
Does that mean I must finish by Thursday night?
items.explanation: “Before Friday” excludes Friday. Checking Thursday night makes the boundary clear.

items.context: A friend says a café is “not bad.” You are unsure how positive that is.
items.prompt: Ask how they rate the café.
options: Do you mean it is your favourite café?
Do you mean you would never go there again?
Do you mean you have not visited it yet?
Do you mean it is quite good, or only okay?
items.explanation: “Not bad” can express different degrees of approval. Ask instead of assuming strong praise.

items.context: You think an instruction means “send one copy,” but the wording is unclear.
items.prompt: Check that interpretation.
options: Should I send it to the same address as before?
Do you mean I should send just one copy?
Should I send it today or tomorrow?
Should I send a printed copy or a digital copy?
items.explanation: “Do you mean…?” checks the intended instruction without treating your guess as certain.

items.context: You understand the first part of an explanation, but the final part is unclear.
items.prompt: Identify the part you need help with.
options: Could you tell me when I will need these instructions?
I understand the first part. Could you explain the last part again?
Could you repeat the first part before moving on?
Could you check whether my answer to the first part is right?
items.explanation: Say what you understood and what you still need. This avoids repeating the whole explanation unnecessarily.

items.context: You forget the word “charger,” but you need to borrow one.
items.prompt: Describe the object’s use.
options: Can I borrow the thing you use to hear music from a phone?
Can I borrow the thing you put around a phone to protect it?
Can I borrow the thing you use to charge a phone?
Can I borrow the thing you use to hold a phone upright?
items.explanation: When a word is missing, describe what the object does. A charger supplies power to a phone.

items.context: You need a few seconds to choose your next words.
items.prompt: Keep your turn while you think.
options: Let me think for a moment.
Let me ask for your opinion first.
Let me sum up what you just said.
Let me check that I heard your question correctly.
items.explanation: “Let me think” requests brief thinking time. It does not end the conversation.

items.context: You begin a sentence but realize it is too complicated.
items.prompt: Start the same idea again more simply.
options: Let me put that another way.
Let me return to the previous topic.
Let me add another point to that.
Let me check whether that is correct.
items.explanation: “Put that another way” signals a new wording of the same idea.

items.context: You cannot remember “receipt.” You want proof that you paid.
items.prompt: Describe what you need.
options: Could I have the paper that shows what I still owe?
Could I have the paper that lists the things I can order?
Could I have the paper that explains how to use it?
Could I have the paper that shows I paid?
items.explanation: The purpose of the paper identifies the receipt without needing the exact word.

items.context: You know a word in your first language but not in English. You can explain its meaning.
items.prompt: Ask for the English word after describing it.
options: What did the person say about these water pipes?
When can someone check the water pipes?
What do you call a person who fixes water pipes?
Who can come and fix these water pipes?
items.explanation: “What do you call…?” asks for a name or word. Describing the job gives the listener a useful clue.

items.context: You started to say “cheap,” but you mean something costs a fair amount for its quality.
items.prompt: Correct your word choice.
options: Not exactly cheap—I mean more than I can afford.
Not exactly cheap—I mean available at half its usual price.
Not exactly cheap—I mean good value.
Not exactly cheap—I mean the lowest price available.
items.explanation: “Good value” compares price with what you receive. It does not necessarily mean a low price.

items.context: You know the main idea but not an exact number. You want to avoid inventing one.
items.prompt: Give an honest approximation.
options: I know it is fewer than twenty, but not how many.
I have checked, and the total is twenty.
I don’t know the exact number, but it is about twenty.
I’ll put twenty as the exact number for now.
items.explanation: “About” marks an estimate. Say that the exact figure is unknown.

items.context: You want to describe “a queue,” but cannot remember the word.
items.prompt: Use a short description.
options: There is a list of prices beside the door.
There is a group of chairs near the wall.
There is a stack of boxes under the counter.
There is a line of people waiting to pay.
items.explanation: Describe the people and what they are doing. This communicates the idea of a queue.

items.context: You use a word and then realize it has the wrong meaning. You want to correct yourself immediately.
items.prompt: Signal a correction.
options: Sorry, that is not the word I meant.
Sorry, could you explain the word you used?
Sorry, could you spell my last word for me?
Sorry, could you repeat what you just heard?
items.explanation: Take responsibility for your own word choice. Then replace or explain the word.

items.context: You cannot explain a shape well with words. You have a pen and paper.
items.prompt: Offer another way to show it.
options: Would it help if I gave you the measurements only?
Would it help if I named the material it is made from?
Would it help if I explained what it is used for?
Would it help if I drew it?
items.explanation: A drawing can support a spoken description when the missing information is visual.

items.context: Two people start speaking at the same time. You want the other person to speak first.
items.prompt: Give them the turn.
options: Sorry, go ahead.
Sorry, may I finish my point first?
Sorry, could you start that point again afterward?
Sorry, could we return to the earlier topic?
items.explanation: “Go ahead” invites the other person to continue.

items.context: You are explaining something. Someone interrupts before you reach your main point.
items.prompt: Ask politely to finish your point.
options: Could we leave this point until next time?
Could I finish this point first?
Could you finish your point before I start?
Could you summarize the points so far?
items.explanation: “Could I finish this point?” keeps the request specific and polite.

items.context: A discussion has moved to a new subject. You still have one question about the previous subject.
items.prompt: Return briefly to that subject.
options: Could we discuss the delivery date at our next meeting?
Could we move on from the delivery date now?
Could we go back to the delivery date for a moment?
Could we confirm the new topic before we continue?
items.explanation: “Go back to” returns to an earlier topic. “For a moment” signals a brief return.

items.context: A group is discussing a plan. You want to add a relevant idea.
items.prompt: Join the discussion politely.
options: Could I summarize the ideas we have heard so far?
Could I add one idea?
Could you repeat the idea you just mentioned?
Could I check whether we have agreed on the plan?
items.explanation: “Could I add…?” asks for a turn to contribute something relevant.

items.context: A friend has finished explaining a problem. You want to show that you are listening before asking a question.
items.prompt: Acknowledge what you heard.
options: I see. Shall I tell you what I think happened?
I see. What happened after that?
I see. Would you like to hear about my day now?
I see. Shall we leave the rest for another time?
items.explanation: A short acknowledgement plus a follow-up question encourages the speaker to continue.

items.context: You need to leave a call soon, but the other person is still explaining something.
items.prompt: State your time limit and ask for the main point.
options: I have two more minutes. Shall I explain my own experience?
I have two more minutes. What is the main thing I need to know?
I have two more minutes. Could you repeat every step?
I have two more minutes. Could we discuss another example?
items.explanation: State the limit honestly, then help the speaker choose the essential information.

items.context: Someone asks you a question while you are checking the answer on a screen.
items.prompt: Explain the short delay.
options: One moment, please. I’m checking the details.
One moment, please. Could you ask the question more slowly?
One moment, please. I’d like to add a point of my own.
One moment, please. I’m not sure which question you mean.
items.explanation: Explaining what you are doing makes the pause understandable.

items.context: You want to end a helpful conversation warmly.
items.prompt: Thank the person and close the conversation.
options: Thanks. Could you explain the next step as well?
Thanks. May I check one more detail before we finish?
Thanks. Could we go back to the first question?
Thanks, that answers my question. Have a good day.
items.explanation: Confirm that you have what you need, then use a friendly closing.

items.context: A colleague gives a long explanation. You want to check the key points before moving on.
items.prompt: Introduce a short summary.
options: Let me add my own example before we continue.
Let me check when we can discuss the next topic.
Let me ask you to repeat every detail from the beginning.
Let me check that I have the main points right.
items.explanation: A summary checks understanding and gives the other person a chance to correct it.

items.context: You have answered one question, but you are unsure whether the explanation was useful.
items.prompt: Invite clarification.
options: Shall we move to my next question now?
Does that answer your question, or should I explain more?
Would you like to answer the next question yourself?
Could you tell me why you asked the question?
items.explanation: Offer more explanation without assuming that the listener understood or failed to understand.

items.context: You said the appointment was on Monday. The listener repeats “Tuesday.”
items.prompt: Correct the day clearly and politely.
options: Sorry, would you prefer Tuesday to Monday?
Sorry, could you tell me whether Monday is available?
Sorry, shall I move the appointment to Tuesday?
Sorry, I meant Monday, not Tuesday.
items.explanation: Repeat the intended day and contrast it with the mistaken day.

items.context: Someone thinks you are criticizing their work. You only meant that the instructions were unclear.
items.prompt: Clarify what your comment was about.
options: I meant your work needs clearer instructions.
I meant I would like to review your work again.
I meant the instructions you followed were wrong.
I meant the instructions were unclear, not your work.
items.explanation: Separate the intended subject of the comment from the unintended personal criticism.

items.context: You gave the wrong price: thirty instead of thirteen. You notice immediately.
items.prompt: Correct your own mistake.
options: Sorry, could you choose between thirteen and thirty?
Sorry, would you like a price lower than thirty?
Sorry, I said thirty, but I meant thirteen.
Sorry, I said thirteen, but I meant thirty.
items.explanation: State both the mistaken and correct numbers so the correction is unmistakable.

items.context: A listener thinks you want to cancel. You actually want to move the booking to another day.
items.prompt: Explain the difference.
options: I’d like to cancel and request a refund.
I’d like to make a second booking for another day.
I’d like to change the date, not cancel the booking.
I’d like to keep the date but change the time.
items.explanation: Changing a booking keeps the booking but alters a detail. Cancelling removes it.

items.context: Someone asks, “Do you mean all the files?” You mean only the two attached files.
items.prompt: Limit your request precisely.
options: Just the two attached files, please.
All files from every folder, please.
Any files you find are fine.
No files need to be sent.
items.explanation: “Just” limits the request. Identify which two files you mean.

items.context: You agree with a goal but have concerns about the proposed method.
items.prompt: Show the agreement and the specific concern.
options: I’m still deciding whether the goal is worth pursuing.
I agree with the goal and the method. When do we begin?
I agree with the goal. Could we discuss a different way to reach it?
I agree with the method. Could we choose a different goal?
items.explanation: Separate agreement about the result from uncertainty about how to achieve it.

items.context: Someone thinks your example is a real event from your life. It is an invented example.
items.prompt: Clarify the status of the example.
options: That is something that will happen to me next week.
That is what usually happens in my own experience.
That was just an example, not something that happened to me.
That happened to someone else, rather than to me.
items.explanation: Make it clear that the situation was imagined. An example need not describe a real event.

items.context: You used “we,” and the listener thinks you mean the whole company. You mean your small team.
items.prompt: Explain who “we” refers to.
options: By “we,” I mean all the people who work here.
By “we,” I mean our team and the company’s other teams.
By “we,” I mean our team, not the whole company.
By “we,” I mean you and me only.
items.explanation: Pronouns can have unclear boundaries. Name the group explicitly.

items.context: You said you were “not sure.” The listener treats that as a definite refusal.
items.prompt: Clarify that you have not decided.
options: I haven’t decided yet. I’m not saying no.
I’ve decided not to take part this time.
I’m ready to agree if we start today.
I’d like to withdraw the agreement I gave earlier.
items.explanation: Uncertainty is not the same as refusal or agreement. State that the decision is still open.

items.context: You thought “next Friday” meant one date, but the other person meant another.
items.prompt: Resolve the date without arguing about the phrase.
options: Could we repeat the words “next Friday” once more?
Could we use the exact date to avoid confusion?
Could we confirm whether Friday suits both of us?
Could we choose a different day of the week?
items.explanation: Relative dates can be interpreted differently. An exact date removes that uncertainty.

items.context: Someone asks for information you do not know. You can check it later.
items.prompt: Avoid guessing and offer a next step.
options: I don’t know. Could we discuss a different question?
I’m not sure. I’ll check and get back to you.
I can give you an estimate now, but I cannot check it.
I think I remember the answer, so I’ll use that.
items.explanation: State the limit of your knowledge, then offer to find the information.

items.context: A request is unclear. You need to know whether speed or detail matters more.
items.prompt: Ask the speaker to choose the priority.
options: Would you prefer to discuss this today or tomorrow?
Would you prefer a quick summary or a detailed explanation?
Would you prefer an email or a phone call?
Would you prefer my opinion or the customer’s opinion?
items.explanation: Present the relevant alternatives. This helps you match the answer to the person’s needs.

items.context: You cannot meet a request by today, but you can complete it tomorrow morning.
items.prompt: State the limit and offer a realistic alternative.
options: I can send a rough version today and finish it next week.
I can’t finish today, but I can send it tomorrow morning.
I can send it later today once it is complete.
I can send it tomorrow, but I cannot say which part of the day.
items.explanation: A clear limit and a specific alternative help the conversation move forward.

items.context: You disagree with a suggestion and want to explain your reason respectfully.
items.prompt: Choose a response that opens discussion.
options: I see your point. Could you repeat the suggestion?
I see your point. Let’s decide before discussing the concerns.
I see your point. My concern is the extra travel time.
I see your point. I’m happy to proceed with that plan.
items.explanation: Acknowledge the point, then identify a concrete concern. Agreement is not required for respectful discussion.

items.context: Someone asks a personal question you would rather not answer. You want to keep talking about the task.
items.prompt: Set a boundary and return to the task.
options: I’d rather hear your answer to that question first.
I’d rather answer briefly before returning to the schedule.
I’d rather keep that private. Could we return to the schedule?
I’d rather discuss that after we finish the schedule.
items.explanation: A polite boundary can be brief. Suggesting the task as the next topic helps the conversation continue.

items.context: You have explained something twice. The listener still looks confused.
items.prompt: Try a different explanation without blaming them.
options: Let me repeat the same explanation exactly as before.
Let me go on to the next point, then we can finish.
Let me check whether you heard the final word correctly.
Let me try a different example.
items.explanation: A new example may make the idea clearer. Repeating faster or blaming the listener does not address the difficulty.

items.context: You are asked to agree to a plan before you have read it.
items.prompt: Ask for time to review it.
options: Could I read the details before I decide?
Could I agree now and read the details later?
Could I decline the plan before reviewing it?
Could you tell the group that I support the plan?
items.explanation: Request the information needed for a decision. This does not promise agreement or refusal.

items.context: You notice that two instructions conflict: keep every page, but remove page three.
items.prompt: Point out the conflict and request clarification.
options: Should I ask someone else to carry out both instructions?
Should I keep page three or remove it? The instructions say both.
Should I remove page three, as I did last time?
Should I keep every page and send the file now?
items.explanation: Identify the exact conflict and ask which instruction to follow.

items.context: A colleague apologizes for a small delay. You want to accept the apology and continue the task.
items.prompt: Choose a calm response that moves things forward.
options: Thanks for letting me know. Could you confirm what time you arrived?
Thanks for letting me know. Shall we start now?
Thanks for letting me know. Could you explain the delay in detail?
Thanks for letting me know. Shall we postpone the task until next week?
items.explanation: Acknowledge the apology or update, then suggest the next practical step.

items.context: You and another person have discussed several options but have not confirmed the final choice.
items.prompt: Check the decision before ending.
options: Before we finish, would you like me to suggest an afternoon option?
Before we finish, are we choosing the morning appointment?
Before we finish, shall we compare the other options again?
Before we finish, how long do morning appointments usually last?
items.explanation: A final confirmation reduces the risk of leaving with different understandings.

activities.name: Meaning Switch
activities.description: Compare sentences and notice how their meanings change.

items.context: A: “I lived here for five years.” B: “I have lived here for five years.”
items.prompt: Which sentence normally connects the five years to the present?
options: B: the person normally still lives here.
A: the person must still live here.
Both say the person will move here soon.
Neither gives any information about time.
items.explanation: The present perfect in B normally describes a period continuing up to now. A presents the five years as a past period.

items.context: A: “When I arrived, the talk started.” B: “When I arrived, the talk had started.”
items.prompt: In which sentence did the talk begin before the arrival?
options: B: the talk was already in progress.
A: the talk was already in progress.
Both say the arrival was before the talk.
Neither places the events in time.
items.explanation: “Had started” places the start before another past event: the arrival.

items.context: A: “She has been to the café.” B: “She has gone to the café.”
items.prompt: Which normally means she went there and has not returned yet?
options: B: she has gone there.
A: she has been there.
Both mean she has never visited it.
Neither says anything about a visit.
items.explanation: “Has gone to” normally describes a trip away from the current place. “Has been to” describes a visit or experience.

items.context: A: “I used to cycle to work.” B: “I am used to cycling to work.”
items.prompt: Which means cycling to work feels familiar?
options: A: cycling is familiar to the speaker now.
Both mean the speaker will learn to cycle.
Neither sentence mentions a regular activity.
B: cycling is familiar to the speaker.
items.explanation: “Am used to” means accustomed to something. “Used to cycle” describes a past habit, normally one that has stopped.

items.context: A: “I was cooking when the phone rang.” B: “I cooked after the phone rang.”
items.prompt: Which says the cooking was already happening when the phone rang?
options: Both say the call came before the cooking.
Neither describes the order of events.
A: the cooking was in progress.
B: the cooking was in progress.
items.explanation: “Was cooking when” gives a background action interrupted by the ring. “After” in B puts the cooking later.

items.context: A: “The bus leaves at nine.” B: “The bus left at nine.”
items.prompt: Which reports a completed departure in the past?
options: B: the bus left at nine.
A: the bus leaves at nine.
Both report a past departure.
Neither can refer to a bus timetable.
items.explanation: “Left” is the past form of “leave.” “Leaves” can describe a regular timetable.

items.context: A: “I have just sent the message.” B: “I am about to send the message.”
items.prompt: Which says the message has not been sent yet?
options: A: the person will send it very soon.
Both say the message was sent long ago.
Both say the message has already arrived.
B: the person will send it very soon.
items.explanation: “About to” describes something expected very soon. “Have just sent” means the sending happened a short time ago.

items.context: A: “She still works here.” B: “She no longer works here.”
items.prompt: Which says her work here continues?
options: Both say she has never worked here.
Both say she will start next week.
A: she works here now.
B: she works here now.
items.explanation: “Still” marks continuation. “No longer” means a previous situation has ended.

items.context: A: “I didn’t finish the form.” B: “I haven’t finished the form yet.”
items.prompt: Which more clearly presents the form as unfinished up to now?
options: Both say it will never be finished.
Neither refers to completing a form.
B: it remains unfinished now.
A: it must be finished now.
items.explanation: “Haven’t finished…yet” connects the unfinished task to now and often suggests it is still expected.

items.context: A: “The train was leaving when we reached the platform.” B: “The train had left when we reached the platform.”
items.prompt: Which says the departure was already complete?
options: A: the train was already gone.
Both say the train had not begun to move.
Neither says anything about departure.
B: the train was already gone.
items.explanation: “Had left” places a completed departure before the arrival. “Was leaving” describes the departure in progress.

items.context: A: “You mustn’t park here.” B: “You don’t have to park here.”
items.prompt: Which says parking here is forbidden?
options: A: parking here is not allowed.
B: parking here is not allowed.
Both forbid parking here.
Neither gives any choice about parking.
items.explanation: “Mustn’t” means not allowed. “Don’t have to” means not necessary; another place may be chosen.

items.context: A: “You should save a copy.” B: “You must save a copy.”
items.prompt: Which gives stronger obligation in an ordinary instruction?
options: Neither suggests saving a copy.
B: saving a copy is required.
A: saving a copy is required.
Both say saving a copy is forbidden.
items.explanation: “Should” commonly gives advice. “Must” expresses a requirement or strong obligation.

items.context: A: “The shop might be open.” B: “The shop is open.”
items.prompt: Which leaves the opening status uncertain?
options: B: the shop may or may not be open.
Both state that the shop is definitely closed.
Neither sentence concerns uncertainty.
A: the shop may or may not be open.
items.explanation: “Might” marks a possibility. B makes a direct claim that the shop is open.

items.context: A: “You may leave now.” B: “You must leave now.”
items.prompt: Which gives permission without requiring departure?
options: Both forbid immediate departure.
A: leaving now is allowed.
B: leaving now is merely allowed.
Both require immediate departure.
items.explanation: “May” can grant permission. “Must” says the action is required.

items.context: A: “I can swim.” B: “I could swim when I was six.”
items.prompt: Which explicitly describes ability at a past age?
options: A: the ability existed only at age six.
Both describe permission to use a pool.
Neither describes swimming ability.
B: the ability existed at age six.
items.explanation: “Could…when I was six” places the ability in the past. A describes present ability.

items.context: A: “You needn’t bring lunch; we provide it.” B: “You shouldn’t bring lunch; food is not allowed inside.”
items.prompt: Which says bringing lunch is unnecessary?
options: A: lunch will be provided.
B: lunch must be brought anyway.
Both say lunch is provided.
Neither explains why lunch is mentioned.
items.explanation: “Needn’t” means there is no need. B advises against bringing food because it is not allowed inside.

items.context: A: “They could arrive today.” B: “They will arrive today.”
items.prompt: Which makes the less certain prediction?
options: B: arrival today is a possibility only.
Both state arrival today is impossible.
Neither mentions a possible arrival.
A: arrival today is a possibility.
items.explanation: “Could” leaves open whether the event will happen. “Will” expresses a firmer prediction here.

items.context: The office lights are on. A: “Someone must be inside.” B: “Someone must go inside.”
items.prompt: Which draws a conclusion from the lights?
options: Both order someone to enter the office.
Neither can express a conclusion.
A: the speaker thinks someone is already inside.
B: the speaker thinks someone is already inside.
items.explanation: “Must be” can express a strong conclusion from evidence. “Must go” here gives an obligation to enter.

items.context: A: “You can’t have sent it; the message is still in Drafts.” B: “You shouldn’t have sent it; it contained a mistake.”
items.prompt: Which says the sending did happen but was a bad idea?
options: Both say the message definitely remained unsent.
Neither refers to a past action.
B: the person sent it and is being criticized.
A: the person sent it and is being criticized.
items.explanation: “Shouldn’t have sent” criticizes a completed action. “Can’t have sent” expresses the conclusion that it did not happen.

items.context: A: “I would help if I had time.” B: “I will help when I have time.”
items.prompt: Which makes help depend on a situation presented as hypothetical?
options: Neither links help to available time.
A: having time is imagined rather than assumed.
B: having time is imagined rather than assumed.
Both promise help immediately.
items.explanation: “Would…if I had” describes a hypothetical condition. B presents future help more directly.

items.context: A: “There are few seats left.” B: “There are a few seats left.”
items.prompt: Which more positively emphasizes that some seats remain?
options: Neither suggests a small number of seats.
B: some seats are available.
A: plenty of seats are available.
Both mean there are no seats at all.
items.explanation: “A few” emphasizes a small available number. “Few” emphasizes how limited the number is.

items.context: A: “We have little time.” B: “We have a little time.”
items.prompt: Which more positively emphasizes that some time remains?
options: Neither refers to available time.
B: there is some time available.
A: there is a great deal of time.
Both mean the task has already finished.
items.explanation: “A little” emphasizes some remaining amount. “Little” emphasizes a shortage.

items.context: A: “Not all the lights are on.” B: “None of the lights are on.”
items.prompt: Which definitely says every light is off?
options: B: no lights are on.
A: no lights are on.
Both definitely say every light is off.
Neither could describe a dark room.
items.explanation: “None” means zero. “Not all” only rules out all of them being on; it does not specify the exact number.

items.context: A: “The bus comes every day.” B: “The bus comes every other day.”
items.prompt: Which describes a bus that comes on alternate days?
options: B: there is a day between services.
A: there is a day between services.
Both describe two services each day.
Neither describes a regular service.
items.explanation: “Every other day” means alternate days, such as Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

items.context: A: “I almost finished.” B: “I finished almost all of it.”
items.prompt: Which definitely says the whole task was completed?
options: Neither says the whole task was completed.
A says the whole task was completed.
B says the whole task was completed.
Both say the whole task was completed.
items.explanation: “Almost” means close to, but not fully. Both leave some part unfinished.

items.context: A: “At least ten people came.” B: “At most ten people came.”
items.prompt: Which allows twelve people to have come?
options: Neither allows more than ten people.
A: ten is the minimum, not the maximum.
B: ten is the minimum, not the maximum.
Both allow twelve people.
items.explanation: “At least” sets a minimum. “At most” sets a maximum.

items.context: A: “I rarely eat out.” B: “I usually eat out.”
items.prompt: Which describes eating out as uncommon?
options: Neither gives information about frequency.
A: it happens infrequently.
B: it happens infrequently.
Both say it never happens.
items.explanation: “Rarely” means not often. “Usually” means it happens in most relevant cases.

items.context: A: “Either entrance is open.” B: “Neither entrance is open.”
items.prompt: You can choose between two entrances. Which statement allows you to enter through either one?
options: Neither statement allows a choice of entrance.
A: both entrances are available.
B: both entrances are available.
Both statements say one entrance is closed.
items.explanation: “Either” allows one or the other here. “Neither” means not one and not the other.

items.context: A: “There is enough space.” B: “There is too much space.”
items.prompt: Which says the amount meets the need without calling it excessive?
options: Both say more space is necessary.
Neither compares space with a need.
A: the space is sufficient.
B: the space is sufficient but not excessive.
items.explanation: “Enough” means sufficient. “Too much” means more than is wanted or suitable.

items.context: A: “I go there twice a month.” B: “I go there every two months.”
items.prompt: Which describes the more frequent visits?
options: A: two visits each month.
B: one visit every two months.
Both describe the same frequency.
Neither tells us how often visits happen.
items.explanation: “Twice a month” is about four times as frequent as one visit every two months.

items.context: A: “Only the manager signed the form.” B: “The manager signed only the form.”
items.prompt: Which limits who signed, rather than what was signed?
options: B: nobody except the manager signed it.
Both limit what the manager signed.
Neither limits any part of the statement.
A: nobody except the manager signed it.
items.explanation: “Only” before “the manager” limits the person. Before “the form,” it limits the thing signed.

items.context: A: “I lent you the book.” B: “I gave you the book.”
items.prompt: Which normally means the book should be returned?
options: B: the book is a loan.
Both always require a return.
Neither can involve a change of possession.
A: the book is a loan.
items.explanation: Lending is temporary. Giving normally transfers the item without expecting it back.

items.context: A: “Can I have another cup?” B: “Can I have the other cup?”
items.prompt: Which points to the remaining cup in a known pair?
options: B: the other cup in the pair.
A: any additional cup from a known pair only.
Both mean every cup in the room.
Neither requests a cup.
items.explanation: “The other” identifies the remaining one in a known set of two. “Another” asks for an additional or different one.

items.context: A: “The children dressed themselves.” B: “The children dressed each other.”
items.prompt: Which says each child put clothes on their own body?
options: B: each child dressed themself.
Both describe helping another child dress.
Neither describes who received the action.
A: each child dressed themself.
items.explanation: “Themselves” returns the action to the doers. “Each other” describes reciprocal help between people.

items.context: A: “This is my own room.” B: “This is our shared room.”
items.prompt: Which emphasizes that the room belongs to or is for one speaker alone?
options: Both emphasize joint use.
Neither says anything about use or possession.
A: the room is the speaker’s own.
B: the room is for one speaker alone.
items.explanation: “My own” emphasizes individual possession or use. “Our shared” emphasizes use by more than one person.

items.context: A: “This bag is yours.” B: “This bag is for you.”
items.prompt: Which clearly states ownership rather than intended recipient?
options: Neither connects the bag with the listener.
A: the bag belongs to you.
B: the bag already belongs to you in every context.
Both say the bag belongs to the speaker.
items.explanation: “Yours” states possession. “For you” can identify an intended recipient or purpose before ownership changes.

items.context: A: “Even the new learner understood.” B: “Only the new learner understood.”
items.prompt: Which says the new learner was the sole person who understood?
options: A: nobody else understood.
Both say nobody else understood.
Neither says the new learner understood.
B: nobody else understood.
items.explanation: “Only” excludes other people. “Even” highlights a result the speaker finds surprising.

items.context: A: “I want the same model.” B: “I want a similar model.”
items.prompt: Which allows a model that is close but not identical?
options: Both require the identical model.
Neither compares models.
B: a similar model is acceptable.
A: a different but similar model is explicitly requested.
items.explanation: “Similar” means alike in some ways. “The same” requires identity in the respect being discussed.

items.context: A: “Everyone is not ready.” B: “No one is ready.”
items.prompt: Which clearly and unambiguously means zero people are ready?
options: Both are equally unambiguous in all contexts.
Neither could mean zero people are ready.
B: no person is ready.
A: zero people are certainly ready.
items.explanation: “No one” clearly means zero. “Everyone is not” can be understood in different ways, so clearer wording helps.

items.context: A: “I also called the hotel.” B: “I called the hotel instead.”
items.prompt: Which suggests the call replaced another action?
options: A: the call replaced every other action.
Both mean the call was an extra action.
Neither says the call happened.
B: the call was an alternative action.
items.explanation: “Instead” marks a replacement or alternative. “Also” adds an action to others.

items.context: A: “I stopped smoking.” B: “I stopped to smoke.”
items.prompt: Which means smoking was the reason for taking a break from another activity?
options: A: the person paused in order to smoke.
Both mean the person gave up smoking.
Neither says anything about stopping.
B: the person paused in order to smoke.
items.explanation: “Stop to do” pauses one activity to do another. “Stop doing” ends the activity named.

items.context: A: “Remember to lock the door.” B: “I remember locking the door.”
items.prompt: Which gives a reminder about an action still to be done?
options: A: locking is the task to remember.
B: locking is the task still to be done.
Both describe a memory of a completed action.
Neither concerns remembering an action.
items.explanation: “Remember to do” means do not forget the task. “Remember doing” recalls a past action.

items.context: A: “Try restarting the phone.” B: “Try to restart the phone.”
items.prompt: Which presents restarting as a possible solution to test?
options: Neither suggests restarting the phone.
A: restart it as an experiment.
B: restarting is presented mainly as a method to test.
Both say the phone has already restarted.
items.explanation: “Try doing” often suggests testing a method. “Try to do” emphasizes making an effort to achieve the action.

items.context: A: “Send it by Friday.” B: “Keep it until Friday.”
items.prompt: Which sets a latest time for sending?
options: Both require sending before Thursday.
Neither gives a time limit.
A: send no later than Friday.
B: send no later than Friday.
items.explanation: “By” gives a deadline. “Until” describes how long a situation or action continues.

items.context: A: “I arrived in time for the talk.” B: “I arrived on time for the talk.”
items.prompt: Which more directly says the arrival matched the scheduled time?
options: Both necessarily mean arrival was early.
Neither says arrival allowed attendance.
B: the arrival was punctual.
A: the arrival was exactly at the scheduled time.
items.explanation: “On time” means at the scheduled or expected time. “In time” means early enough for something.

items.context: A: “I worked during the break.” B: “I worked for an hour.”
items.prompt: Which gives the length of the work period?
options: B: the work lasted an hour.
A: the work lasted exactly an hour.
Both give an exact duration.
Neither mentions a period of work.
items.explanation: “For an hour” gives duration. “During the break” identifies when the work occurred.

items.context: A: “Could you lend me a pen?” B: “Could I lend you a pen?”
items.prompt: Which asks the listener to provide a pen to the speaker?
options: B: the pen moves toward the speaker.
Both offer the speaker’s pen to the listener.
Neither concerns temporary use.
A: the pen moves toward the speaker.
items.explanation: “Lend me” makes the speaker the receiver. “Lend you” makes the listener the receiver.

items.context: A: “I’m looking for the child.” B: “I’m looking after the child.”
items.prompt: Which means taking care of the child?
options: Neither mentions responsibility for a child.
B: the speaker is caring for the child.
A: the speaker is caring for the child.
Both mean searching for the child.
items.explanation: “Look after” means take care of. “Look for” means search for.

items.context: A: “We discussed the problem.” B: “We solved the problem.”
items.prompt: Which says a solution was achieved?
options: A: discussing always means solving.
Both guarantee a solution.
Neither can describe a completed action.
B: the problem was solved.
items.explanation: A discussion can happen without a solution. “Solved” says the problem was successfully dealt with.

items.context: A: “I heard the alarm.” B: “I listened to the recording.”
items.prompt: Which more clearly describes deliberate attention to sound?
options: Neither involves sound.
B: the person intentionally paid attention.
A: hearing always requires deliberate effort.
Both necessarily happened by accident.
items.explanation: “Listen to” emphasizes paying attention. “Hear” can happen without deliberate effort.

items.context: A: “We’ll walk unless it rains.” B: “We’ll walk even if it rains.”
items.prompt: Which says rain will not stop the walk?
options: B: the walk will happen despite rain.
A: the walk will happen despite rain.
Both say rain will cancel the walk.
Neither mentions rain as relevant.
items.explanation: “Even if” says the result still applies under that condition. “Unless” introduces an exception.

items.context: A: “Take a coat in case it gets cold.” B: “Take a coat because it is cold.”
items.prompt: Which describes preparation for a possible later problem?
options: Neither gives a reason for taking a coat.
A: the cold is a possibility to prepare for.
B: the cold is only a future possibility.
Both say the weather is warm and will stay warm.
items.explanation: “In case” prepares for a possibility. “Because it is cold” gives a present reason.

items.context: A: “Although it rained, we went out.” B: “Because it rained, we went out.”
items.prompt: Which presents the outing as unexpected in view of the rain?
options: Both give rain as the reason for going out.
Neither says whether the outing happened.
A: the outing happened despite the rain.
B: the outing happened despite the rain.
items.explanation: “Although” marks a contrast. “Because” gives a reason.

items.context: A: “Leave now; otherwise, you’ll miss the bus.” B: “Leave now; then you can catch the bus.”
items.prompt: Which states the consequence of not leaving now?
options: Neither relates departure time to the bus.
A: failing to leave now risks missing the bus.
B: failing to leave now guarantees catching it.
Both state the same consequence of waiting.
items.explanation: “Otherwise” introduces what happens if the preceding instruction is not followed.

items.context: A: “You can borrow it as long as you return it today.” B: “You can borrow it for as long as you need.”
items.prompt: Which makes returning it today a condition?
options: Both allow an unlimited borrowing period.
Neither grants permission to borrow.
A: borrowing depends on a same-day return.
B: borrowing depends on a same-day return.
items.explanation: “As long as” can mean “provided that.” “For as long as” here describes a duration.

items.context: A: “I spoke quietly so that the baby would sleep.” B: “I spoke so quietly that nobody heard me.”
items.prompt: Which states the purpose of speaking quietly?
options: Both describe only unintended results.
Neither links quiet speech with an outcome.
A: the aim was to let the baby sleep.
B: the aim was explicitly to be unheard.
items.explanation: “So that” introduces a purpose here. “So quietly that” describes a degree and its result.

items.context: A: “If I see the notice, I’ll tell you.” B: “When I see the notice, I’ll tell you.”
items.prompt: Which more clearly leaves seeing the notice uncertain?
options: B: seeing it is a condition, not assumed.
Both state that the notice has already been seen.
Neither promises to tell the listener anything.
A: seeing it is a condition, not assumed.
items.explanation: “If” leaves the event uncertain. “When” normally treats it as expected in this future context.

items.context: A: “Despite the delay, we finished on time.” B: “Because of the delay, we finished late.”
items.prompt: Which sentence presents a result that overcame a problem?
options: Both say there was no delay.
A: the delay did not prevent an on-time finish.
B: the delay did not prevent an on-time finish.
Both say the delay caused a late finish.
items.explanation: “Despite” introduces a problem that did not prevent the result. “Because of” explains the reason for the late finish.

items.context: A: “We left early to avoid traffic.” B: “We left early and avoided traffic.”
items.prompt: Which states an intention without guaranteeing success?
options: A: avoiding traffic was the aim.
B: avoiding traffic was only an unconfirmed aim.
Both guarantee that traffic was avoided.
Neither explains anything about traffic.
items.explanation: “To avoid” gives a purpose. B directly states that the traffic was avoided.

items.context: A: “The road may be closed, so check first.” B: “The road is closed, so use another route.”
items.prompt: Which recommends checking because the key fact is uncertain?
options: Both state the closure as an established fact.
Neither offers any advice about what to do.
A: the closure is possible but unconfirmed.
B: the closure is possible but unconfirmed.
items.explanation: “May be closed” leaves uncertainty. A therefore asks for a check before acting.

activities.name: Ask the right question
activities.description: Choose a clear question that asks for the information you need.

items.context: “The parcel is beside the front door.”
items.prompt: Ask about the parcel’s location.
options: When did the parcel arrive?
What is in the parcel?
Where is the parcel?
Whose parcel is it?
items.explanation: “Where” asks about a place. Keep “is” before the subject in this direct question.

items.context: “The blue bag belongs to my sister.”
items.prompt: Ask who owns the bag.
options: Which bag belongs to your sister?
Whose bag is it?
Who does the bag belong?
Who is the bag belong to?
items.explanation: “Whose” asks about possession. “Whose bag” stays together as a phrase.

items.context: “The guide will meet us.”
items.prompt: Ask which person will meet you.
options: Who will meet us?
Who will we meet?
Who does will meet us?
Who we will meet?
items.explanation: “Who” is the subject of this question. It replaces “the guide” before “will meet.”

items.context: “I bought a notebook.”
items.prompt: Ask what the person bought.
options: What did you buy?
What did you bought?
What you bought?
Why did you buy a notebook?
items.explanation: After “did,” use the base form “buy.” The order is “What + did + you + buy?”

items.context: “We are waiting outside the museum.”
items.prompt: Ask where the people are waiting.
options: Where you are waiting?
Where do you waiting?
Who are you waiting for?
Where are you waiting?
items.explanation: With “are waiting,” move “are” before “you” in the direct question.

items.context: “The red folder is mine, not the green one.”
items.prompt: Ask the person to identify their folder.
options: Which folder is yours?
Which folder is your?
Which folder belongs you?
Whose folder is green?
items.explanation: “Which folder” asks for a choice among folders. “Yours” means belonging to you.

items.context: “The box contains spare keys.”
items.prompt: Ask about the contents of the box.
options: What does the box contain in?
What are in the box?
What is in the box?
Where is the box?
items.explanation: “What is in…?” asks what a container holds.

items.context: “I work with the new assistant.”
items.prompt: Ask about the person’s work partner.
options: Who does you work with?
Who works for you?
Who do you work with?
Who you work with?
items.explanation: With “you,” use “do” and the base form “work.” The final “with” is natural in this question.

items.context: “The key opens the side gate.”
items.prompt: Ask what the key opens.
options: Which key opens the side gate?
What does the key open?
What does the key opens?
What do the key open?
items.explanation: “The key” is singular, so use “does.” The main verb stays “open.”

items.context: “I left my coat on the bus.”
items.prompt: Ask where the person left their coat.
options: Where did you leave your coat?
Where did you left your coat?
Where you left your coat?
When did you leave your coat?
items.explanation: “Did” marks the past, so use “leave,” not “left,” after it.

items.context: “The class starts at half past six.”
items.prompt: Ask for the starting time.
options: What time the class starts?
What time do the class start?
What time does the class start?
What time does the class starts?
items.explanation: Use “does” with the singular “class,” followed by the base form “start.”

items.context: “The journey takes forty minutes.”
items.prompt: Ask about the length of the journey.
options: How far is the journey?
How often do you make the journey?
How much does the journey cost?
How long does the journey take?
items.explanation: “How long” asks about duration. “How far” asks about distance.

items.context: “The station is three kilometres away.”
items.prompt: Ask about the distance to the station.
options: How often does the train stop there?
How much is a ticket to the station?
How far is the station?
How long does it take to reach the station?
items.explanation: “How far” asks for distance, such as kilometres or miles.

items.context: “I go swimming twice a week.”
items.prompt: Ask how often the person swims.
options: How often do you go swimming?
How long do you go swimming for?
How far do you swim each time?
How many pools do you use?
items.explanation: “How often” asks about frequency. “Twice a week” answers that question.

items.context: “We need six chairs.”
items.prompt: Ask for the number of chairs needed.
options: How many chairs do we need?
How much chairs do we need?
How many chair do we need?
Which chairs do we need?
items.explanation: Use “how many” with a countable plural noun such as “chairs.”

items.context: “We need two litres of milk.”
items.prompt: Ask about the amount of milk.
options: How much milk do we need?
How many milk do we need?
How much milk we need?
How many cartons of juice do we need?
items.explanation: “Milk” is normally uncountable. Use “how much milk,” or ask “How many litres?”

items.context: “The ticket costs twelve pounds.”
items.prompt: Ask for the ticket price.
options: How much does the ticket costs?
How much the ticket costs?
How much does the ticket cost?
How many does the ticket cost?
items.explanation: For a price, use “how much.” After “does,” use “cost.”

items.context: “The library is closed on Sundays.”
items.prompt: Ask which day the library is closed.
options: What time does the library close?
How long is the library closed for?
Why is the library closed?
Which day is the library closed?
items.explanation: “Which day” asks for a day such as Sunday. “What time” would ask for a clock time.

items.context: “I have worked here since March.”
items.prompt: Ask how long the person has worked there.
options: How long have you worked here?
How long did you worked here?
How long has you worked here?
How long you have worked here?
items.explanation: The present perfect connects the work to now. Put “have” before “you.”

items.context: “We must send the form no later than Friday.”
items.prompt: Ask specifically for the final deadline.
options: Since when must we send the form?
For how long must we send the form?
How often must we send the form?
By when must we send the form?
items.explanation: “By when” asks for the latest allowed time. “For how long” asks about duration.

items.context: “She drives to work every morning.”
items.prompt: Ask whether she drives to work.
options: Does she drives to work?
Do she drive to work?
Is she drive to work?
Does she drive to work?
items.explanation: Present simple questions use “does” with “she” and the base form “drive.”

items.context: “They visited the gallery yesterday.”
items.prompt: Ask whether they visited the gallery yesterday.
options: Did they visited the gallery yesterday?
Do they visited the gallery yesterday?
Were they visit the gallery yesterday?
Did they visit the gallery yesterday?
items.explanation: “Did” carries the past tense. Use “visit” after it.

items.context: “The door is locked.”
items.prompt: Ask whether the door is locked.
options: Does the door locked?
Is locked the door?
Does the door is locked?
Is the door locked?
items.explanation: With “is,” form the question by putting “is” before “the door.”

items.context: “You can use this printer.”
items.prompt: Ask for confirmation of that permission.
options: Do I can use this printer?
Can I using this printer?
May I lend you this printer?
Can I use this printer?
items.explanation: Use “can” directly before the subject, followed by the base verb “use.”

items.context: “The guests are arriving now.”
items.prompt: Ask whether the guests are arriving now.
options: Do the guests arriving now?
Are arriving the guests now?
Is the guests arriving now?
Are the guests arriving now?
items.explanation: The plural subject “guests” takes “are.” Keep “arriving” after the subject.

items.context: “You have received the invitation.”
items.prompt: Ask whether the person has received the invitation.
options: Have you receive the invitation?
Has you received the invitation?
Have you received the invitation?
Do you have received the invitation?
items.explanation: Present perfect questions use “have/has + subject + past participle.” Here: “Have you received…?”

items.context: “The train will stop here.”
items.prompt: Ask whether the train will stop here.
options: Will the train stops here?
Where will the train stop?
Will the train stop here?
Does the train will stop here?
items.explanation: Put “will” before the subject and use the base form “stop.”

items.context: “There are spare batteries in the drawer.”
items.prompt: Ask whether spare batteries are available there.
options: Do there have spare batteries in the drawer?
Is there any spare batteries in the drawer?
Are there a spare battery in the drawer?
Are there any spare batteries in the drawer?
items.explanation: Use “Are there…?” with a plural noun. “Any” is natural in this yes-or-no question.

items.context: “He was reading when you called.”
items.prompt: Ask what he was doing when you called.
options: What was he doing when I called?
What did he doing when I called?
What he was doing when I called?
What were he doing when I called?
items.explanation: Past continuous questions put “was” before “he.” The main verb takes “-ing.”

items.context: “You would prefer a window seat.”
items.prompt: Ask the person which seat they would prefer.
options: Which seat would you prefer?
Which seat do you would prefer?
Which seat would you preferred?
Which seat you would prefer?
items.explanation: After “would,” use the base form “prefer.” In a direct question, “would” comes before “you.”

items.context: “The wind broke the window.”
items.prompt: Ask what caused the window to break.
options: What did the window break?
What broke the window?
What did broke the window?
What the window broke?
items.explanation: “What” replaces the subject “the wind.” No extra “did” is needed in this ordinary subject question.

items.context: “The wind broke the window.”
items.prompt: Ask which thing the wind broke.
options: What the wind did break?
What did the wind break?
What broke the wind?
What did the wind broke?
items.explanation: Here “the wind” remains the subject. Use “did” to ask about the object.

items.context: “Someone has taken the umbrella.”
items.prompt: Ask who took the umbrella.
options: Who the umbrella has taken?
Who has taken the umbrella?
Who have taken the umbrella?
Who did has taken the umbrella?
items.explanation: “Who” is the subject, followed by “has taken.”

items.context: “The teacher called the driver.”
items.prompt: Ask which person the teacher called.
options: Who did the teacher called?
Who the teacher called?
Who did the teacher call?
Who called the teacher?
items.explanation: “Who did the teacher call?” asks about the receiver of the call. “Who called the teacher?” reverses the roles.

items.context: “Three students need another worksheet.”
items.prompt: Ask how many students need one.
options: How many worksheets does each student need?
How many students need another worksheet?
How many students does need another worksheet?
How many students needs another worksheet?
items.explanation: The phrase “How many students” is the plural subject. Use “need” without an extra “do.”

items.context: “One of these keys opens the cupboard.”
items.prompt: Ask which key opens it.
options: Which key open the cupboard?
Which cupboard does the key open?
Which key opens the cupboard?
Which key does opens the cupboard?
items.explanation: “Which key” is a singular subject, so the present simple verb is “opens.”

items.context: “I spoke to the receptionist.”
items.prompt: Ask which person the speaker spoke to.
options: Who you spoke to?
Who spoke to you?
Who did you speak to?
Who did you spoke to?
items.explanation: Use “did you speak,” not “did you spoke.” Ending with “to” is natural here.

items.context: “The delay caused the problem.”
items.prompt: Ask what the delay caused.
options: What caused the delay?
What did the delay caused?
What the delay caused?
What did the delay cause?
items.explanation: Keep “the delay” as the subject. “What caused the delay?” asks a different question.

items.context: “The people near the door have tickets.”
items.prompt: Ask which people have tickets.
options: Which people has tickets?
Which people do has tickets?
How many tickets do the people need?
Which people have tickets?
items.explanation: “Which people” is a plural subject. Use “have.”

items.context: “A broken cable stopped the machine.”
items.prompt: Ask what stopped the machine, not what the machine stopped.
options: What did the machine stop?
What did stopped the machine?
Why did the machine stop the cable?
What stopped the machine?
items.explanation: The cause is the subject. Replace it with “what” and keep “stopped the machine.”

items.context: You want to ask a stranger where the nearest station is.
items.prompt: Choose a correctly formed polite question.
options: Could you tell me which station opens earliest?
Could you tell me where the nearest station is?
Could you tell me where is the nearest station?
Could you tell me where the nearest station?
items.explanation: Inside “Could you tell me…,” use statement order: “where the station is.”

items.context: You need to know when the office opens.
items.prompt: Complete a polite question correctly.
options: Do you know when the office open?
Do you know why the office opens late?
Do you know when the office opens?
Do you know when does the office open?
items.explanation: The inner question uses statement order and the ordinary verb form: “the office opens.”

items.context: You are unsure whether the café accepts cards.
items.prompt: Ask politely whether cards are accepted at all, without assuming that they are.
options: Could you tell me which cards the café accepts?
Could you tell me whether the café accepts cards?
Could you tell me whether does the café accept cards?
Could you tell me whether the café accept cards?
items.explanation: “Whether” introduces a yes-or-no question inside another question. Use “the café accepts.”

items.context: You want to know the current price of a ticket you plan to buy.
items.prompt: Ask about the current price in a correctly formed indirect question.
options: Could you tell me why the ticket costs more today?
Could you tell me how much the ticket costs?
Could you tell me how much does the ticket cost?
Could you tell me how much the ticket cost?
items.explanation: For the current price, use “the ticket costs” inside the indirect question. “The ticket cost” would ask about a past price. “Does the ticket cost” uses direct-question order.

items.context: You want to ask why a service was cancelled.
items.prompt: Choose a correct question after “Do you know…”
options: Do you know when the service was cancelled?
Do you know why the service was cancelled?
Do you know why was the service cancelled?
Do you know why did the service cancel?
items.explanation: Use statement order inside the larger question: “the service was cancelled.”

items.context: You need to find out which entrance to use.
items.prompt: Choose a clear, correct request for guidance.
options: Could you show me where the entrance sign was made?
Could you show me which entrance to use?
Could you show me which entrance use?
Could you show me which entrance to using?
items.explanation: “Which entrance to use” is a natural shortened way to ask for guidance.

items.context: You want to know if a room is available.
items.prompt: Choose a correct indirect question.
options: Do you know if the room is available?
Do you know if is the room available?
Do you know if the room available?
Do you know why the room is unavailable?
items.explanation: With “if,” put the subject before the verb: “the room is available.”

items.context: You want directions to the exit.
items.prompt: Choose a correct question after “Can you tell me…”
options: Can you tell me how get to the exit?
Can you tell me how to getting to the exit?
Can you tell me when the exit is locked?
Can you tell me how to get to the exit?
items.explanation: “How to get to…” asks for the steps or route needed to reach a place.

items.context: You need to ask who is responsible for the booking.
items.prompt: Choose a correct polite question.
options: Could you tell me who the booking is for?
Could you tell me who is responsible for the booking?
Could you tell me who does responsible for the booking?
Could you tell me who responsible for the booking?
items.explanation: Here “who” is the subject of “is responsible,” so that order remains unchanged.

items.context: You want to know when a package will arrive.
items.prompt: Choose a correct indirect question.
options: Do you know when the package will arrive?
Do you know when will the package arrive?
Do you know when the package will arrives?
Do you know where the package will arrive?
items.explanation: Use “the package will arrive” inside the indirect question. Do not move “will” before the subject.

items.context: “The repair will be ready soon.” You need a specific collection time.
items.prompt: Ask for the missing time.
options: How often do you repair this model?
Why did you choose that repair method?
What time will it be ready for collection?
What kind of repair did you do?
items.explanation: “Soon” is vague. Asking for a collection time turns it into a practical detail.

items.context: “I travelled with my neighbour.” You want to know the companion’s identity.
items.prompt: Ask about the companion, not the destination.
options: When did you travel back?
Who did you travel with?
Where did you travel to?
How did you travel there?
items.explanation: “Who…with?” asks for the companion. The other questions ask where, how, or when.

items.context: “I have two brothers. The older one lives abroad.”
items.prompt: Ask which brother lives abroad.
options: Where were your brothers born?
When did both brothers move abroad?
Which of your brothers lives abroad?
How many brothers do you have?
items.explanation: “Which of” selects a person from the known group. The statement does not say both moved abroad.

items.context: “The course runs from May to July.” You need to know how many classes happen each week.
items.prompt: Ask about weekly frequency.
options: How many classes are there each week?
How many months does the course last?
Which month does the course start?
Which month does the course finish?
items.explanation: The dates give the overall period, not the number of weekly classes.

items.context: “The lift is out of order.” You need another way to reach the second floor.
items.prompt: Ask for an alternative route.
options: When will the lift be working again?
How long does the lift normally take?
Which floors does the lift usually serve?
How can I get to the second floor without the lift?
items.explanation: Your goal is reaching the floor. Ask how to do that without the unavailable lift.

items.context: “The price includes delivery.” You want to know whether installation is included too.
items.prompt: Ask only about installation.
options: Does the price also include installation?
Does the price include delivery?
How much does delivery cost separately?
Can delivery be arranged for a different day?
items.explanation: “Also” adds the new service to the one already confirmed. Repeating the delivery question adds no new information.

items.context: “We need the document before lunch.” You do not know when lunch starts.
items.prompt: Ask for a clock time.
options: What time do you need the document by?
How long will you need to keep the document?
Which parts of the document do you need?
How soon after lunch can you return the document?
items.explanation: A clock-time deadline is clearer than “before lunch” when the lunch time is unknown.

items.context: “You can choose a small or large locker.” Your bag is 70 centimetres long.
items.prompt: Ask for information that helps it fit.
options: How many bags can I store in each locker?
How long is each locker inside?
How much does each locker cost to use?
How long can I keep a bag in a locker?
items.explanation: The inside length helps you compare the locker with the bag. Price and time limits do not tell you whether it will fit.

items.context: “The road is closed between the bridge and the school.” Your destination is beyond the school.
items.prompt: Ask for useful travel guidance.
options: Which side of the school has a visitor entrance?
When does traffic usually become busy near the school?
Which route can I take around the closed section?
How long does it usually take to cross the bridge?
items.explanation: You need a route around the closure. The other details do not answer that travel problem.

items.context: “The instructions say to send the original.” You have a paper document and a scan.
items.prompt: Check which form is required.
options: Do you need it this week, or would next week be acceptable?
Do you need the paper original, or is a scan acceptable?
Do you need the first draft, or the revised wording?
Do you need the full document, or only the summary?
items.explanation: Contrast the two possible forms explicitly. This checks the requirement without assuming that a scan is acceptable.

activities.name: Story builder
activities.description: Put four sentences in a clear order by choosing the right sequence.

items.title: A spare key
items.context:
A. I reached the door and discovered that I had no key.
B. I used it to open the door.
C. She brought the spare key to the door.
D. I called my neighbour to ask for the spare key.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: A → C → D → B
A → D → B → C
A → D → C → B
D → A → C → B
items.explanation: The missing key causes the call. The neighbour must bring the spare before it can open the door.

items.title: Making tea
items.context:
A. After the tea had brewed, I removed the bag.
B. I filled the kettle with cold water.
C. When it boiled, I poured the water over the tea bag.
D. I switched it on and waited for the water to boil.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: B → D → A → C
B → D → C → A
D → B → C → A
B → C → D → A
items.explanation: The water is put in the kettle before heating. The tea brews after the hot water is added.

items.title: A parcel at the counter
items.context:
A. I took the notice and my identification to the counter.
B. I received a notice saying that my parcel was at the collection counter.
C. I carried the parcel home.
D. The clerk checked them and handed me the parcel.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: B → A → C → D
B → A → D → C
A → B → D → C
B → D → A → C
items.explanation: The notice prompts the visit. The parcel is handed over before it can be carried home.

items.title: An empty bottle
items.context:
A. I noticed that my water bottle was empty.
B. I found a drinking-water tap in the hall.
C. I put the full bottle in my bag.
D. I filled the bottle at that tap.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: B → A → D → C
A → D → B → C
A → B → C → D
A → B → D → C
items.explanation: The empty bottle creates the need to find water. It must be filled before it is described as full.

items.title: Replacing a battery
items.context:
A. I closed the cover and checked that the clock was running.
B. I put a new battery in the empty space.
C. The clock stopped, so I opened its battery cover.
D. I removed the old battery.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: C → B → D → A
C → D → A → B
C → D → B → A
D → C → B → A
items.explanation: Opening the cover allows removal. The new battery goes in after the old one comes out.

items.title: Returning a library book
items.context:
A. I placed it in the return slot.
B. I put the book in my bag and walked to the library.
C. The next day, my account showed that the book had been returned.
D. A reminder told me that my library book was due.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: B → D → A → C
D → A → B → C
D → B → C → A
D → B → A → C
items.explanation: The reminder leads to the trip. The account update follows the physical return.

items.title: Buying bread
items.context:
A. When it was my turn, I asked for a loaf.
B. The assistant put the loaf in a bag and told me the price.
C. I paid and took the bag.
D. I joined the queue at the bakery.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: D → B → A → C
D → A → C → B
D → A → B → C
A → D → B → C
items.explanation: Joining the queue comes before being served. The price is given before the described payment.

items.title: A forgotten umbrella
items.context:
A. I found the umbrella under the chair.
B. As I left the café, I realized my umbrella was still inside.
C. I picked it up and left the café again.
D. I went back to my table.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: B → D → C → A
B → D → A → C
D → B → A → C
B → A → D → C
items.explanation: The realization causes the return. Finding the umbrella precedes picking it up.

items.title: Washing a shirt
items.context:
A. After the wash finished, I hung the wet shirt up.
B. I noticed a stain on my shirt and took it off.
C. When it was dry, I put it away.
D. I put the shirt in the washing machine.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: B → D → C → A
B → D → A → C
D → B → A → C
B → A → D → C
items.explanation: The wash must finish before the shirt is hung up. Drying comes before putting the dry shirt away.

items.title: Setting an alarm
items.context:
A. I learned that I had to leave home early the next day.
B. I got up when I heard it.
C. The next morning, the alarm rang at six.
D. I set my alarm for six o’clock.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: A → C → D → B
A → D → B → C
A → D → C → B
D → A → C → B
items.explanation: The early departure explains setting the alarm. The alarm must ring before the speaker responds to it.

items.title: A platform change
items.context:
A. An announcement said that the train would leave from platform four instead.
B. I was waiting on platform two for my train.
C. The train arrived there, and I boarded it.
D. I followed the signs to platform four.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: B → A → D → C
A → B → D → C
B → D → A → C
B → A → C → D
items.explanation: The announcement changes the plan. The traveller reaches the new platform before boarding there.

items.title: A missed bus
items.context:
A. I checked the timetable for the next bus.
B. It showed a twenty-minute wait, so I sat on the bench.
C. When the next bus arrived, I got on.
D. I reached the stop just as my bus drove away.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: A → D → B → C
D → B → A → C
D → A → C → B
D → A → B → C
items.explanation: Missing the bus prompts the timetable check. The waiting period comes before the next bus arrives.

items.title: Finding a hotel
items.context:
A. She told me to turn left after the bridge.
B. I asked a shopkeeper for directions.
C. I followed her directions and found the hotel.
D. I came out of the station but could not find my hotel.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: D → B → C → A
D → B → A → C
B → D → A → C
D → A → B → C
items.explanation: The directions are requested and given before the traveller follows them.

items.title: A bicycle repair
items.context:
A. I walked the bicycle to a repair shop.
B. The mechanic repaired the tyre while I waited.
C. I rode the repaired bicycle home.
D. My bicycle tyre went flat on the way home.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: D → B → A → C
D → A → C → B
D → A → B → C
A → D → B → C
items.explanation: The flat tyre prevents riding. The repair must be completed before the bicycle is ridden home.

items.title: An earlier train
items.context:
A. I boarded the earlier train with the same ticket.
B. The clerk confirmed that I could use it.
C. I arrived at the station an hour earlier than planned.
D. I asked whether my ticket was valid on an earlier train.
items.prompt: Which order tells the story clearly from start to finish?
options: C → D → B → A
D → C → B → A
C → B → D → A
C → D → A → B
